If you aren't a specific user in this thread, you are shadowbanned. It is wrong to think of either of intermolecular forces as "bonds"; they are more like interactions. I like to think of all the intermolecular forces as a rating system. Some molecules can hydrogen bond, some have dipoles, and some have other forces.  That being said, these forces arise when a molecule does not have any electrostatic activity. Molecules do not like to touch each other, so these forces ensure that they do not.  I am not sure you quite what you mean by polar bond, as it really isn't an intermolecular force. It is just a way to categorize a bond. For example, H-O is a polar bond because the O is very electronegative and pulls electron density away from hydrogen.  C-H is not a polar bond because there isn't really any major difference in electronegativity to have a considerable effect. That being said, if you take two CH3 molecules and put them around each other, they will still interact when close enough because there *is* electric activity, just not enough to make the bond polar. I hope that helps.

That's what I was trying to get across by saying how I thought of the intermolecular forces as a rating system. How you "start" with weaker forces and go up to different types of intermolecular forces (H bonds, dipoles, etc). I don't have any stats, but let's work through this together. Let's say you're studying a professional field at a decent school getting decent grades. You apply for internships your later years and you work in the summer for a large firm or some sort of company. You make connections and your resume is built up and you have something to take to an interview. Instead of when the interviewer asks you, "what do you know about the professional field?" and you respond with, "well, I know from in school that.... *BUT I WOULD BE REALLY INTERESTED TO WORK WITH THEM*..." you can say, "Yeah, I learned about them in school, and then I learned from my experience with ___ for __ months, that they're actually more like ___ and I really actually enjoy working with them and found a real knack for it." You can apply that to any business degree. Science degrees, too. Hell, maybe even a communications degree. But with certain humanities degrees... what the hell do you think you can *DO* for a job with that? Why would any employer hire somebody who has zero experience with anything that this future employee may do? Sure, you can train someone with that degree to do anything someone with a business degree can (I think degrees are kind of just formalities and you learn the most from experience) do, but why would an employer risk it? I'm sure there are stats out there on this... but that's just using some common sense and experience to apply to this "feeling" I have.
